summary: In this article, we use the PBNF-transform, or Polynomial Boolean Normal Form, described in the two earlier articles and now extended to higher arity, to solve Boolean satisfiability problems (SAT), which are part of the P versus NP problem. SAT consists of a conjunction of clauses, and in our SAT-solving models, we dualize the logical equations by inverting the problem: we multiply letters (literals) in the transferred clauses and use a binary iterated composition based on adding polynomials for the conjunctions in our solution formula. We obtain Polynomial Boolean Equations, PBE=0, by also renaming the truth value T=0. With reversed literal repetition, we get the CNF as the sum of the transformed clauses. In fact, we can always reduce to multiplication in and addition out of clauses, as we do not look for the entire kernel of PBE for a YES instance for SAT.

summary: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.
title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design

summary: Trial-and-error FE simulation of sheet forming could be computationally expensive, neural-network-based learned simulators are used to accelerate design. These simulators should accurately capture localised responses, such as thinning around sharp radii or near ribs, which determine formability. Transformer-based neural operators propagate information efficiently across the mesh but tend to smooth such localised responses. This study develops BiLoGo, a Bipartite Local-Global learned simulator with an FE-guided design that connects local node-element message passing with a Transformer-based neural operator for long-range information exchange. BiLoGo has three modules: a bidirectional node-element GraphSAGE model that learns nodal-elemental coupling on a bipartite graph and predicts each quantity on its native FE entity without interpolation; a dual-stream Transformer-based neural operator that processes blank deformation and tool contact with separate token sets, preventing localised contact information from being averaged with the whole-blank state; and a fusion and element update module that combines global and local features via gated residual fusion and updates element features conditioned on element-node kinematics. Evaluated on a dome-shaped cold forming case and two corner-shaped hot stamping cases (one with ribs), BiLoGo achieves the lowest positional and threshold-based thinning errors on all three cases compared with single-level and hierarchical graph-based models and Transformer-based neural operators. Near the ribs, the smoothing index of predicted thinning increases from 0.41-0.56 for Transformer-based neural operators to 0.94 for BiLoGo-U. Compared with the hierarchical graph network CAtt-BiUGNN, BiLoGo-T reduces mean positional error by 15.5% on the Corner case and BiLoGo-U by 8.3% on the Corner+Rib case, with 66-69% less training memory.
title: BiLoGo: Reducing the smoothing of localised responses in Transformer-based neural operators for sheet forming

summary: Large Language Model training is increasingly constrained by memory capacity. Activation Checkpointing reduces activation memory by avoiding storing selected activations during the forward pass and rematerializing them during backpropagation, thereby trading memory savings for additional computation. Although this technique is essential for scaling model training, rematerialization can be prohibitively expensive, particularly for Transformer linear layers. Approximate computation could reduce this overhead, but conventional approaches either introduce errors that accumulate over the backward pass or fail to exploit information available from the initial forward pass. We introduce a novel approximate rematerialization method that can yield unbiased gradient estimates: using information collected during the initial forward pass, the method selectively recomputes only the most important layer components, either through greedy selection or randomized sketching. Ablation studies show that the resulting gradients closely match the exact gradients. When applied to feed-forward layers, attention layers, or both, our method can recompute only two-thirds of the layer components in a Llama-488M model, while increasing perplexity by just 1.7%, 1.2%, and 2.5%, respectively.
title: Know What You Need: Efficient Activation Checkpointing

summary: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and dynamic range for uncooperative spacecraft pose estimation, but models trained on synthetic event streams must generalize to the noise, background activity, and contrast variation of physical sensors. We present a comparative systems study of two independently developed approaches to synthetic-to-real, event-based 6-DoF spacecraft pose estimation. The first is a modular pipeline that combines learned keypoint detection and unlabeled target-domain adaptation with geometry-based pose recovery and temporal smoothing. The second directly regresses translation and rotation from global and cropped event representations using an apparent-scale cue, physics-motivated synthetic corruptions, and feature-consistency regularization. We evaluate both systems under the same SPARK 2026 hidden-test protocol on the real-event split of SPADES, with predictions for all test frames. The results reveal a component-wise reversal concealed by the aggregate challenge score: direct regression reduces orientation error by 22.7% (1.1767 to 0.9101 rad) and obtains a 13.4% lower composite score, whereas the modular pipeline reduces relative translation error by 78.7% (0.1335 to 0.0285). Archived configurations and a qualitative failure case identify plausible explanations for these complementary error profiles, without isolating their causes. These findings motivate a testable hybrid design that combines direct orientation estimation with geometry-constrained translation recovery.
title: Direct Regression and Geometric Recovery for Event-based Spacecraft Pose Estimation

summary: We study weighted edge boundary and outer vertex boundary on Cayley graphs of polynomial growth of degree $Q>1$. For every finite symmetric generating set, we prove that each exact isoperimetric profile satisfies $I(n)=c n^{(Q-1)/Q}+O(n^{(Q-1)/Q-β})$, where $β=1/(8Q^2)$. We identify the leading constant with the isoperimetric constant of a horizontal perimeter on the limiting Carnot group, after accounting for the counting density. Its integrand is a norm with polyhedral unit ball, determined by a convex minimization with one real variable for each coset of a torsion-free nilpotent subgroup. For every asymptotically minimizing sequence, we translate its vertex sets so that the characteristic functions of the associated rescaled regions are precompact in $L^1$. The limiting regions minimize continuum perimeter at fixed volume. The exact-cardinality estimate requires no regularity assumption on these regions. For virtually abelian groups, we prove a quantitative stability estimate using a discrete approximation to the Euclidean Wulff body. The relative symmetric difference from a translate is bounded by the square root of the sum of the relative boundary deficit and a cardinality error. We also characterize when bounded additive changes of Cayley metric preserve the leading vertex constant. Failure occurs already in rank two; we construct pairs with the same measured asymptotic cone whose leading constants have an unbounded ratio as the rank grows.
title: Sharp isoperimetry in groups of polynomial growth

summary: Behind the expanding use of large language models (LLMs) across application domains lies a growing dependence on specialized GPU kernel libraries. These libraries underpin the correctness and efficiency of training and inference across diverse GPU platforms, implementing attention, GEMM, quantization, and low-precision operators while managing tensor shapes, memory layouts, code generation, and hardware-specific dispatch. Problems at this layer can silently corrupt outputs, hang GPUs, prevent compilation, introduce deployment incompatibilities, or degrade performance, thereby reducing developer productivity and wasting expensive GPU resources. We present the first comprehensive empirical study of issues in GPU kernel libraries for LLM systems. We manually analyzed 300 high-quality GitHub issue reports, their discussions, and available fixes from seven representative libraries: FlashInfer, FlashAttention, Triton, CUTLASS, DeepGEMM, xFormers, and bitsandbytes. The analysis characterizes symptoms, root causes, fixes, and testing and debugging practices. Our main findings are: (1) 60.33% of the sampled issues originate in the Compiler and Build System or Runtime Environment dimensions, so validation must cover the deployment and execution stack, not just kernel code. (2) Kernel specialization imposes implicit correctness constraints on tensor shapes, metadata layouts, memory aliasing, and hardware resources. Violations can produce incorrect outputs or launch failures even for supported operations, highlighting the need for explicit contract validation and boundary-case testing. (3) Current testing and debugging practices are often insufficient for identifying low-precision numerical problems and hardware-specific execution failures. We outline research opportunities and tooling directions to support future LLM GPU kernel development.
title: An Empirical Study of Issues in GPU Kernel Libraries for LLM Systems

summary: Existing Korean benchmarks for Large Language Models (LLMs) evaluate performance across diverse knowledge domains, but their accuracy scores cannot distinguish whether incorrect responses arise from a lack of required knowledge or a failure to apply that knowledge correctly. Our analysis of existing Korean benchmarks reveals that most questions can be answered through factual recall alone, while those demanding greater application also differ in required knowledge, making it difficult to isolate application ability. To address this, we introduce KLEAR, a framework that constructs knowledge-matched contrasts by varying application demand while preserving the required knowledge. During construction, KLEAR identifies the knowledge underlying each source question as an explicit anchor bundle to guide generation of questions requiring more complex application. Generated candidates then undergo automated and human validation, with iterative revision based on evaluation feedback. Experiments demonstrate that the resulting knowledge-matched sets largely satisfy the intended constraints, enabling controlled evaluation across diverse LLMs. These evaluations reveal that increasing application demand exposes failures that persist even when the required knowledge is provided.
title: KLEAR: Knowledge-Matched LLM Evaluation in Korean across Application Requirements via Controlled Benchmark Transformation

summary: Multi-agent systems become capable through institutional mechanisms, such as rules that route information to agents that act on it. These mechanisms are also natural places to restrict the system. Yet as agents learn, share memory, delegate, and repair failures, the collective can find other paths to the same effects: a restriction on the original mechanism still operates but no longer stops them, while routine performance and compliance checks pass. We propose \textbf{Reversible Multi-agent Systems} as a research agenda: collectives that grow while an authorized supervisor can still restrict specified effects, keep them restricted as agents adapt, and reconstitute useful cooperation under renewed authority. What is reversed is the ability to produce a specified effect; restrictions must hold even if learned knowledge persists. The goal is to preserve effective intervention, not a particular mechanism: at every step of growth, some authorized intervention must keep a specified prohibited effect rare while maintaining required service. We identify three research problems: tracking what capabilities depend on, handing off control before an old mechanism loses its effect, and separating legitimate repair from unauthorized reconstruction. We outline how to evaluate control across growth paths, back control claims with evidence, and allocate the rights to restrict and restore.
title: From Emergence to Reversibility: Toward Reversible Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Walsh analysis connects ordered Fourier convergence, summability, nonlinear approximation, and universal representation through a common character algebra. This survey examines developments from 2000-2026 against their classical foundations. Binary kernel geometry explains Hardy-space losses and summability thresholds; interval and packet methods control spectral selection; localized blocks produce correction and universal representations with distinct coefficient and exceptional-set requirements. Selected proofs and counterexamples compare these mechanisms and identify where an implication needs an additional hypothesis. The same distinctions organize digital integration, sparse measurements, Boolean spectra, and generalized Walsh bases. Quantitative thresholds, source conventions, and published theorem pointers are collected in comparative tables. The concluding problems separate source-listed questions, proposed refinements, and elementary obstructions. Supplementary derivations preserve normalization checks and finite covariance calculations while keeping the main exposition focused on the analytic mechanisms.
title: Walsh Analysis in the Twenty-First Century: Convergence, Summability, Nonlinear Approximation, Universality, and Digital Applications

summary: A germination study of Peltophorum africanum seeds was conducted in the laboratory of the Department of Crop Science and Production, Botswana University of Agriculture and Natural Resources from May to June 2017. Seeds were collected from Butale and Gaborone to assess effect of pre-sowing treatments on germination. The experiment followed a completely randomized design (CRD) with five treatments; control, boiling water, hot water, mechanical scarification and concentrated sulphuric acid. The boiling water treatment had three different levels of time exposure, while the sulphuric acid had four different levels of time exposure. Seed germination percentages, germination mean time and germination index were significantly ( P < 0.0001) affected by pre-sowing treatment methods. The maximum germination percentages (82-87) of Butale seeds were recorded in the mechanical scarified seeds, seed immersed in hot water and all sulphuric acid soaking times. The maximum germination percentages (75-88) in the Gaborone seeds were recorded in mechanical scarification, immersion in hot water, boiling water (1min) and sulphuric acid. Mechanical scarification and hot water are methods recommended for use by tree growers and farmers to break dormancy P. africanum because the acid is expensive and need trained people. published by the Journal of Biodiversity and Environmental Sciences | JBES
title: Effects of different pre-Sowing treatments on germination of Peltophorum africanum Sond seeds from two provenances in Botswana

summary: Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support commonly focus on the clinical appropriateness of individual responses, potentially overlooking failures that emerge across extended interactions. As AI assistants accumulate memory of users' circumstances and prior disclosures, this raises an accountability question: Do AI chatbots provide appropriate support as users' needs evolve? We investigate by analyzing 14,256 longitudinal simulations grounded in donated chatbot histories from 22 users, examining how a memory-equipped assistant responds to suicidal ideation, self-harm, and anxiety crises across recovery trajectories and communication styles. We introduce the Context-Aware and Readiness-Evaluative (CARE) framework, developed with mental health professionals, to assess the timing and quality of advice, including omissions. Advice was less aligned with users' readiness after a crisis than in matched control stretches of the same conversation, largely because of premature recommendations, which were most common when recovery stalled. Revisiting a crisis reduced premature advice but not lagging advice, and users' communication style changed how often and when the assistant gave recommendations. Although explicitly unproductive advice was rare, the assistant frequently omitted clinician-expected support such as follow-up and planning for next steps. These findings show the limits of single response-level safety evaluation and the need to assess timing, omission, and consistency across users when holding AI systems accountable for longitudinal support.
title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Evaluating Timing and Omission in Longitudinal AI Mental Health Support

summary: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query. Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.
title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents

summary: Tendon-driven continuum robots can reach through constrained spaces, but contact along their bodies is invisible to the sensors at their motors. We show that this is a structural limitation rather than a tuning problem: the map from contact forces to tendon measurements has a null space of dimension at least seven, so no estimator that leaves the contact support free can locate contact. When the obstacle geometry is known, however, non-penetration and complementarity make the contact force locally identifiable, and we prove that the resulting system with unknown contact inputs is locally exponentially strongly detectable. We present a constrained moving horizon estimator (MHE) that encodes these conditions and runs in real time as one quadratic program per sample, and we give a local, mode-wise robust stability result for it. In a finite- element benchmark of a two-section robot pressing and sliding on a wall, the estimator located contact to 0.9 mm and estimated contact force to 0.22 N, compared with 65 mm and 0.72 N for a tuned extended Kalman filter (EKF) with state projection. The estimator tolerated millimeter- level errors in the obstacle position and unmodeled wall friction, under which the projected EKF failed. Under randomized model mismatch over 40 trials, including unmodeled tendon friction, it remained better in force and location in every trial. Without contact, the MHE offered no advantage over the EKF, which confirms that its benefit comes from the contact constraints. This report extends a letter submitted to IEEE Control Systems Letters with complete proofs and additional experiments.
title: Locating Contact on Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots From Tendon Measurements Alone via Constrained Moving Horizon Estimation

summary: The pigs were bleeding. That was the point of the experiment: could airway pressure reveal hemorrhage before it became critical? In the UCR Time Series Classification Archive, the de facto benchmark for Time Series Classification (TSC), the same recordings ask a different question: "which of 52 pigs produced this trace?". The dataset PigAirwayPressure is not an outlier. Although the archive is the standard benchmark, whether its tasks resemble the problems TSC is meant to solve has rarely been examined. We find that several datasets are repurposed from their original task, built from toy setups, or have flawed test splits. We further question how representative the archive's ordered non-temporal sequences (e.g. spectra, shape outlines) are of real TSC, and the potential downsides from the decomposition of multivariate problems. Our findings call for more careful interpretation of archive-wide scores and greater attention to deployment-relevant evaluation. The audit is at https://github.com/automl/ucr-provenance-audit.
title: Fifty-Two Shades of Pig: What the UCR Archive Really Asks Classifiers to Do

summary: Recommendation systems often enter a new serving window before enough outcomes are available to retrain the deployed model. We study this regime with 0.05-1.0% target feedback, a range that spans our stress tests while keeping supervision far below the degrees of freedom of the source recommender. At this scale, existing fine-tuning and meta-learning methods still estimate target-specific updates from extremely sparse feedback, leaving the update direction weakly identified. SAGE-PAIR instead transfers a source-supported residual correction space and only calibrates this space using target outcomes. We introduce SAGE-PAIR, a staged adapter that pretrains a low-dimensional global residual on an adjacent source period and adds a soft router over residual experts conditioned on source user profiles. Target feedback then calibrates this residual state rather than relearning the recommender. On a locked test split of KuaiSAR-v2, SAGE-PAIR (Full) achieves a 1.77% relative improvement in NDCG@10, while a core-protocol comparison shows a further 0.25% gain from routed experts beyond source-pretrained PAIR. Matched source-pretrained LoRA and Adapter-Tuning baselines remain near the source model, supporting the need for a different adaptation space. Thus, SAGE-PAIR improves ranking quality with millisecond-scale adaptation and inference costs. Sparse-feedback adaptation is fundamentally governed by the identifiability of the update space rather than by label count alone. Source pretraining supplies estimable correction directions for scarce labels, while user-conditioned routing contributes a consistent, differentiated cross-user correction on top of the global correction. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SAGE-PAIR-610E/.
title: SAGE-PAIR: Source-Pretrained Routed Residual Adaptation for Sparse-Feedback Recommendation

summary: We propose a fixed-point acceleration method for optimization over probability measures, applicable to a variety of machine learning problems. We represent probability measures as pushforwards of a reference distribution through a neural network map and equip the parameter space with the induced pullback Wasserstein metric. This geometric structure allows natural gradient descent to be interpreted as a fixed-point iteration on a Riemannian manifold. We accelerate this iteration using Riemannian Anderson mixing method, which exploits historical residuals to capture approximate second-order information without forming Hessians. In the present parametric setting, the manifold is represented by Euclidean coordinates endowed with a point-dependent metric, simplifying retraction and vector transport. We evaluate the method on multimodal sampling, PDE-based inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling. Across the tested tasks, Anderson mixing reduces the number of natural-gradient iterations and achieves competitive performance relative to SGD and Adam in terms of both loss-gradient evaluations and wall-clock time. These results suggest that fixed-point acceleration is an efficient tool for improving the computational efficiency of training on parametric Wasserstein methods.
title: Fixed-point acceleration on Neural Wasserstein manifolds

summary: Overview The script conducts the full end-to-end inferential and descriptive statistical analysis pipeline reported in the manuscript . It evaluates changes in commercial drivers' subjective states (sleepiness, physical fatigue symptoms, musculoskeletal discomfort, and blood pressure) alongside objective sustained attention measured via the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) before and after simulated driving sessions . Statistical Pipeline & Methodology Pre-Post Subjective Comparisons: Calculates median and interquartile ranges (Q1, Q3), Wilcoxon signed-rank test statistics, paired rank-biserial correlation effect sizes, and one-sample Hodges-Lehmann median difference estimates paired with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (5,000 resamples) . Fatigue Symptoms & Musculoskeletal Discomfort: Evaluates discrete fatigue symptoms using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm-Bonferroni family-wise error rate corrections, and assesses anatomical discomfort changes across individual Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ) regions using exact McNemar tests . Objective Vigilance (PVT): Analyzes pre-to-post alterations in median reaction time (RT), mean RT, mean reciprocal reaction time (1/RT), fastest 10% RT, slowest 10% RT, lapses (RT >= 500 ms), and false starts, adjusted via Holm corrections . Cross-Domain Concordance & Associations: Computes Spearman rank correlations with 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals (4,000 resamples), partial Spearman correlations controlling for prior sleep duration, and Cohen's kappa coefficient to quantify concordance across elevated symptom domains . Subjective Fatigue vs. Objective Vigilance: Tests associations between subjective self-reports and objective vigilance metrics with Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) adjustments, complemented by Kruskal-Wallis tests across composite elevated impairment levels . Sensitivity Power Analysis: Computes the minimal detectable paired Cohen's d effect size and minimal detectable correlation coefficient (|rho|) achievable at 80% statistical power and an alpha level of 0.05 . Files & Data Structure analisis_TSR.py : Standalone Python replication script . Input Data: Expects an Excel workbook named Dataset_Induk_n20_v2.xlsx containing participant records within the sheet named data . Generated Output: Automatically writes all formatted statistical output tables directly into a consolidated Excel file named Hasil_Analisis_TSR.xlsx . Execution & Reproducibility Deterministic Randomness: All resampling routines utilize a fixed pseudorandom number generator seed ( seed = 2026 ) to ensure exact reproducibility across runs . Execution: Run directly via terminal/command line: python analisis_TSR.py or within a Google Colab notebook by placing Dataset_Induk_n20_v2.xlsx in the active runtime directory and invoking !python analisis_TSR.py . Software Requirements The script prints active package versions directly to the console upon execution for reporting in manuscript methodology sections . Required dependencies: Python NumPy pandas SciPy statsmodels scikit-learn
title: Replication code for: "Driver subjective responses and objective vigilance after simulated truck driving"

summary: Reproducibility archive for the Reviews of Geophysics commissioned review on anthropogenic heat in urban climate systems. It holds the evidence base behind the review and the machinery that produced it. The deposit is organised as five bundles, so a reader can take only the part they need: rog-ah-01-search-and-corpus : the locked Web of Science query, its per-branch counts, and the corpus index that screening ran over. rog-ah-02-prompts-and-schema : the screening and extraction prompts with their changelog, and the JSON schemas used to validate model output. rog-ah-03-model-runs : one directory per model run: inputs, outputs, and metadata recording the model identifier and prompt version, together with the structured per-paper extraction. rog-ah-04-figure-data-and-scripts : inputs, plotting scripts and the source manifest behind the figures, including the one compared dataset that has no persistent identifier. rog-ah-05-si-counts : the scripts that derive the counts reported in the supporting information, the reduced audit records they read, and the derived values. title: Reproducibility archive for Anthropogenic Heat in Urban Climate Systems: Forcing, Sensitivity, and Feedback

summary: How does using less conversational history change reader-token use and benchmark scores? We examine this question on 1,100 BEAM questions. We held the retrieval ranking and reader constant across five fixed passage budgets, and mean assigned scores rose as the passage budget grew. The score gain per additional token became smaller at the upper tested budgets. Answerable questions generally received higher scores with more context. Pooled abstention scores sometimes rose as the passage budget shrank. We also tested message retention in a controlled task with explicit conversational-state targets and compared retained user messages with token-matched recency. Qwen matched the full state more often for direct requirements when user messages were retained. Its full-state matching declined when answers depended on references to earlier offers. Mistral produced near-floor results across the retention conditions. A scoring audit leaves the correctness of BEAM answers unresolved. These experiments characterize the token and score consequences of the tested memory budgets. Reliable budget selection depends on retaining the evidence each question requires and validating the measure used to assess answer quality.
title: How Much Conversation History Does an AI Agent Need?

summary: Private, personalised language models must run on local consumer devices, where large, frontier models cannot fit, and retaining long contexts is non-trivial. Sequential memory---the key-value (KV) cache---grows linearly with context length, quickly dwarfing the model itself: for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, 200,000 retained entries require 21 GiB, 6.6 times more than the model weights. Yet the KV-cache compression methods we measured fail beyond moderate compression ratios. We introduce Transformer-FSQ, addressing extreme KV-cache compression by replacing standard key and value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck. Our cache stores a packed vector of discrete integer codes per token, with no per-token quantisation metadata. Converting a pretrained transformer trains only these projections on 0.25 tokens per original parameter. We evaluate Transformer-FSQ against five baseline families on models from 0.6B to 8B parameters. On long-context retrieval (RULER), from 12$\times$ to 97.5$\times$ Transformer-FSQ is the most accurate method we evaluate, across scales. A fused Triton kernel decodes directly from the integer codes; with baselines given their authors' kernels where available, it decodes at $1.01\times$ (95% interval $0.98$--$1.05$) the throughput of native SDPA attention on the uncompressed Qwen3-8B-Base at $32\times$ and $1.54\times$ at $97.5\times$. Extreme KV-cache compression is therefore a practical way to extend how much context a fixed device can hold.
title: Transformer-FSQ: Discrete Latents for Extreme KV-Cache Compression

summary: Language-model agents use experience through external retrieval and parameter learning. Consolidating stored experience into model weights requires deciding both which experience to train on and when its external records can leave retrieval. Admission based solely on student mastery can exclude useful teacher demonstrations, while removal immediately after training can discard guidance that the model still needs. We introduce ENGRAM, a framework that separates training admission from memory release. A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or sufficient successful teacher demonstrations. The student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph (ETG). A verification gate then compares the updated model without episodic retrieval against the base model with retrieval on reserved probes. Release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria; records for skills that fail verification remain retrievable. Experiments across interactive and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over frozen-weight ETG controls, with ablations supporting demonstration-aware admission and selective adapter activation. A controlled held-out comparison shows that verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while remaining close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate and budget-matched random release. ENGRAM also improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls. Skill-level verification further reduces retrievable experience through selective archival, retaining external guidance for skills that do not meet the release criteria. Code is available in anonymous.4open.science/r/engram-anonymous.
title: ENGRAM: From Agent Experience to Weights through Verified Consolidation

summary: We establish an exact curved-background Weyl double copy for the doubly spinning Pomeransky--Sen'kov black ring. Its full Weyl tensor is a quadratic form in two source-free Maxwell fields: one generated by the stationary Killing vector, the other a flux-carrying magnetic field obtained by linearizing the dipole-ring gauge potential about its vacuum limit. The mixed Maxwell bilinear is essential: no spacetime-independent real or complex change of field basis removes it. We identify the inverse $S_{IJ}$ of the Weyl coefficient matrix as a matrix zeroth copy. The same matrix arises independently from a weighted limit of the inner products of two Killing vectors in a six-dimensional Ricci-flat parent and satisfies $\Box_g S_{IJ}=-\tfrac12 F_{I\,ab}F_J{}^{ab}$. The singly spinning limit recovers the diagonal two-field Weyl double copy of the Emparan--Reall ring.
title: The Double Copy of the Doubly Spinning Black Ring

summary: Editing a video stream in real time, without access to future frames, is essential for interactive applications. Existing training-free video editing methods, however, assume full offline access to the entire sequence, while streaming approaches either rely on additional training or are limited to specific editing techniques. We show that this limitation can be removed by analyzing the self-attention dynamics of DMD-distilled autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models. We uncover a key asymmetry: queries and keys remain stable and aligned with their source counterparts across denoising timesteps, while values diverge and encode the evolving content. Inherited from the non-distilled bidirectional teacher, this asymmetry is strongest at high noise, where few-step streaming models operate. The resulting mechanism is simple: a single forward pass suffices to capture source identity in the value features, which can be reused throughout generation. Starting from pure Gaussian noise and injecting only these source values reconstructs the input with fidelity matching or surpassing inversion-based methods, effectively eliminating inversion. Based on this insight, we introduce AR-Edit, a training-free, inversion-free method that caches source values once and selectively injects them during denoising. Across multiple AR backbones, AR-Edit enables real-time streaming editing with superior source preservation and tonal fidelity at minimal overhead.
title: AR-Edit: Training-Free Autoregressive Video Editing without Inversion

summary: We consider Box-Cox transformations of correlation matrices, $Φ_α(C)=\mathrm{vecl}\{(C^α-I)/α\}$, with Jacobian $J_α$. The family nests the raw correlations at $α=1$, the generalised Fisher transformation (GFT), $C\mapsto\mathrm{vecl}(\log C)$, at $α=0$, and the negated off-diagonal concentration coordinates at $α=-1$. The inverse problem is a strictly convex program for every $α$, so every member is injective. The map is onto $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, $d=n(n-1)/2$, if and only if $α\le0$, such that $α=0$ defines the boundary for unrestricted parametrizations. For $α>0$ the image is bounded. The conditioning obeys the bound $κ(J_α)\leκ(C)^{|1-α|}$, where $κ(C)=λ_{\max}(C)/λ_{\min}(C)$, and on the surjective range the exponent is smallest at $α=0$. Under Gaussian sampling with $n\geq3$, the asymptotic covariance of the transformed sample correlations is the identity at independence for every member, but only $α=0$ retains the identity to first order in the correlations, whereas the leading joint third cumulant at independence vanishes only at $α=1/3$. Finally, applying the transformation to the diagonal rescaling of $C$ that makes the result hollow adds a new family to the existing correlation parametrizations. For every $α$ the rescaling solves a strictly convex problem and the inverse is explicit, and the scaled coordinates are unrestricted exactly when $α=0$, where they recover the known global normal coordinates, centred at independence, for the efficient information metric of the correlations.
title: Box-Cox Transformations of Correlation Matrices

summary: Given an arbitrary function $f:[N]\to[M]$, the function inversion problem asks to preprocess $f$ and to be able to, when given some $y\in [M]$, decide whether there exists some $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$ and if so, to report such an $x$. Recently, Fiat-Naor's solution to this problem has seen significant traction in theoretical computer science, and allowed for several conjectures related to meta-complexity and the 3SUM problem to be broken. In this paper, we consider the natural extension of the function inversion problem that we call preimage reporting. Here, instead of having to report only one $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$, the whole set $f^{-1}(y)$ must be found. We present a new general method to convert any arbitrary function inversion scheme into an efficient corresponding preimage reporting scheme. In particular, if $Δ$ is the maximal indegree of $f$, we show that we can perform preimage reporting using space $S$ in time $T$ for any $T$ and $S$ satisfying $TS^2=N^2 Δ$, matching a variant of a tradeoff obtained by Fiat and Naor for function inversion. This last result implies an improvement over the corresponding function inversion scheme itself, which constitutes the first function inversion scheme whose query time is inversely proportional to $|f^{-1}(y)|$. We derive new simple solutions for the $k$SUM-indexing with reporting and Jumbled indexing with reporting problems.
title: From Function Inversion to Preimage Reporting

summary: We study a Bayesian inverse problem in EUV reflectometry, where optical constants and layer thicknesses are inferred from angle- and wavelength-resolved reflection measurements. The physical process is modeled and evaluated using an efficient forward model based on the transfer matrix method. As an alternative to computationally expensive sampling-based inference, we employ an Eulerian, entropically regularized Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme that minimizes the Kullback--Leibler divergence via proximal steps in the Wasserstein space. Using the Benamou--Brenier dynamic formulation and a Hopf-Cole transform, each JKO step is reformulated as a pair of heat equations coupled only through their initial and terminal conditions, enabling an efficient fixed-point solver. The resulting high-dimensional densities are discretized on tensor-product grids and represented in tensor-train format, exploiting Kronecker structure for scalable computation. Preconditioning based on estimated posterior moments further improves tractability. We test the method with numerical experiments on EUV reflectometry data for a ruthenium--silicon ($\ce{Ru}$ on $\ce{Si}$) specimen and compare the learned tensor-train posterior to ensemble Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) reference samples. We demonstrate a use case in which we are able to reuse the tensor-train posterior to obtain samples for shifted target distributions with less computational effort than a comparable MCMC method.
title: Bayesian Inverse Problems for EUV reflectometry with regularized JKO scheme

summary: Local response measurements track how perturbations spread in quantum simulators and nonequilibrium many-body systems. Locality bounds constrain the propagation speed, but do not determine whether the response can distinguish computational outcomes at fixed measurement precision as the distance increases. Here we construct time-independent dynamics with bounded nearest-neighbor interactions in which a fixed single-site detector responds to a remote bond phase after a time proportional to their separation. The susceptibility has a positive lower bound independent of distance. With product-state preparations, estimating this susceptibility to constant additive accuracy is complete for bounded-error quantum polynomial time (BQP), with a decision gap independent of distance. Two source-phase settings give the susceptibility with a distance-independent shot count at fixed accuracy and confidence. Inverse-polynomially weak local couplings between the computational register and the chain carrying the excitation preserve the gap. The leading correction vanishes when exchanging the two internal states of the excitation reverses the interaction. Varying the source and observation time makes all bond phases locally identifiable near the zero-phase reference setting. We also prove a conditional quantum advantage for distribution-free response prediction.
title: BQP-Complete Susceptibilities Observable at Ballistic Times in Local Quantum Dynamics

summary: In this article, we use the PBNF-transform, or Polynomial Boolean Normal Form, described in the two earlier articles and now extended to higher arity, to solve Boolean satisfiability problems (SAT), which are part of the P versus NP problem. SAT consists of a conjunction of clauses, and in our SAT-solving models, we dualize the logical equations by inverting the problem: we multiply letters (literals) in the transferred clauses and use a binary iterated composition based on adding polynomials for the conjunctions in our solution formula. We obtain Polynomial Boolean Equations, PBE=0, by also renaming the truth value T=0. With reversed literal repetition, we get the CNF as the sum of the transformed clauses. In fact, we can always reduce to multiplication in and addition out of clauses, as we do not look for the entire kernel of PBE for a YES instance for SAT.
title: SAT Solving by Multiplication in and Addition out of Clauses

summary: Trial-and-error FE simulation of sheet forming could be computationally expensive, neural-network-based learned simulators are used to accelerate design. These simulators should accurately capture localised responses, such as thinning around sharp radii or near ribs, which determine formability. Transformer-based neural operators propagate information efficiently across the mesh but tend to smooth such localised responses. This study develops BiLoGo, a Bipartite Local-Global learned simulator with an FE-guided design that connects local node-element message passing with a Transformer-based neural operator for long-range information exchange. BiLoGo has three modules: a bidirectional node-element GraphSAGE model that learns nodal-elemental coupling on a bipartite graph and predicts each quantity on its native FE entity without interpolation; a dual-stream Transformer-based neural operator that processes blank deformation and tool contact with separate token sets, preventing localised contact information from being averaged with the whole-blank state; and a fusion and element update module that combines global and local features via gated residual fusion and updates element features conditioned on element-node kinematics. Evaluated on a dome-shaped cold forming case and two corner-shaped hot stamping cases (one with ribs), BiLoGo achieves the lowest positional and threshold-based thinning errors on all three cases compared with single-level and hierarchical graph-based models and Transformer-based neural operators. Near the ribs, the smoothing index of predicted thinning increases from 0.41-0.56 for Transformer-based neural operators to 0.94 for BiLoGo-U. Compared with the hierarchical graph network CAtt-BiUGNN, BiLoGo-T reduces mean positional error by 15.5% on the Corner case and BiLoGo-U by 8.3% on the Corner+Rib case, with 66-69% less training memory.
title: BiLoGo: Reducing the smoothing of localised responses in Transformer-based neural operators for sheet forming

summary: Deep learning training is difficult to verify within a scientific workflow: its architecture, hyperparameters, and procedure are rarely fixed until training has been attempted, and two honest runs never produce the same weights, so recomputation cannot serve as a check. We present SciCheck, a framework in which the scientist explores training configurations freely and posts a blueprint to a provenance ledger for each candidate they want verified, and a verifying scientist judges the resulting run in two layers: a statistical judge model that compares per-step gradient statistics against the verifier's own reference run, and a spot-check that re-executes randomly chosen training segments whose checkpoints are committed to the ledger one epoch at a time. On an MLP, a CNN, and an autoencoder at 100k-500k parameters, under gradient sign flipping, label poisoning, and fabricated runs, SciCheck reaches F1 of 0.966, 0.906, and 0.976 while rejecting 0-4.4% of honest runs. For the attacks we test, the spot-check accounts for most of this accuracy, and we characterize what each layer can detect. The effective-signal statistic falls as $(1-2s)^2$ under a sign flip of severity $s$, so gradient statistics alone catch strong enough sign flips, while fabricated runs that replay genuine statistics look no more anomalous than honest runs to any statistical detector we test. The spot-check catches fully fabricated segments with probability at least $1-(1-s)^k$ for $k$ sampled segments when the draws stay hidden until the run is committed, which roughly matches our measurements and lets a verifier choose $k$ for a target soundness. Verification costs 1.5-2.3x one retraining, mostly for the verifier's reference run; each submission's spot-check takes under 1.5 s, and per-epoch commitments reduce checkpoint storage 5-17x compared with keeping every checkpoint.
title: SciCheck: A Framework for Verifying the Integrity of Deep Learning Training

summary: The natural environments habitable to life are inseparable from dissipative and entropic forces, which mandate active matter to operate on constant fluxes of energy and momentum to survive and propagate through spacetime. In contrast to fundamental particles which are characterized by energy and momentum, we postulate that energy expenditure rate and momentum generation rate are the fundamental dynamical quantities driving this evolution of swimming active matter and accordingly construct the corresponding Lagrangian and Hamiltonian of motion of the active matter. Finally, we formalize the bidirectional coupling between active swimmers and the surrounding fluid via a multipole expansion of the active force with an emphasis on force monopoles and dipoles, where each pole corresponds to a distinct mode of active motility.

summary: Abstract In most AI-agent and automation stacks, one component decides and a downstream component simply trusts that decision. A policy engine, gateway, classifier, trusted execution environment or approval step says yes. The tool, MCP server, database, cloud API or payment rail then carries out whatever request arrives with that approval. This leaves several gaps: the checker may be the same component that collected the inputs; approvals, tokens and receipts can be replayed, widened, rerouted or used after policy has changed; the operation that was checked can differ from the one actually committed, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap; personal and enterprise data, once readable, can be indexed, embedded, joined, exported, used for training or used to steer an agent without any explicit authorization for that use. Under GDPR purpose limitation and the EU AI Act’s expectations for oversight and cybersecurity, these gaps are exactly where controls are needed. Today they are mostly covered by policy, logging and after-the-fact audit. This disclosure describes a two-instance execution-control architecture that removes the single point of trust: First check, at collection time. A first protected domain binds inputs, instructions, provenance, purpose, jurisdiction, scope and permitted effect when the data arrives. An input integrity gateway seals provenance first, so poisoned inputs are refused binding. Second, independent check, at execution time. A second protected domain validates the proposed action against that binding. It is independent through a separate hardware root, session, keys, runtime or administration. It produces evidence cross-committed to the binding, so neither artifact alone can authorize anything. Release only on agreement. Only when both artifacts mutually corroborate is a single-use, non-bearer authority released. The endpoint checks what is actually happening. At the execution boundary, the endpoint independently reconstructs the actual pending operation through its own attested observation channel. Endpoints include: a tool dispatcher, MCP or connector gateway, or API gateway; a database commit or cloud control plane; cross-border data egress, a payment rail or an actuator. What the endpoint reconstructs. It reconstructs recipient, purpose, jurisdiction, data category and the actual operation. It checks these against both artifacts and against its own state (nonce, counter, spent-capability, and its own policy and revocation epochs). Atomic commit. The endpoint commits the operation atomically, as exactly the operation it verified. Contained compromise. A compromise of either domain, the transport channel or the compute plane is confined to its own window and cannot by itself make an unauthorized act effective. Mismatches fail closed before the effect, not through rollback afterwards. Readable but inert data. Data, agent memories and retrieved documents can remain stored and readable while staying operationally inert. They cannot be indexed, embedded, exported, served, used for training or used to influence a tool call unless that specific use is authorized. Chained evidence. Evidence produced at the endpoint becomes a required input to the next step, and chained validation receipts provide a verifiable record at every point. Shared, not central, authority. Distributed partial shares can replace any central authority, so no single party ever holds a complete reusable authorization. The 54 claims, 15 of them independent, cover: AI-agent tool dispatch; MCP and connector supply-chain substitution; computer-use and browser actions; memory and RAG inertness; multi-agent delegation chains; autonomous cloud-control changes; regulated AI output release by purpose, jurisdiction and recipient; coding and CI/CD agents; agent skills and marketplace extensions; multimodal assistants; voice and meeting agents with consent and recording checks; agentic purchasing; persistent AI memory; workspace and schedule

summary: This repository contains the analysis code accompanying the SPiCe paper (Genome Biology; secrierlab/SPiCe). It has three components. (i) merfish_analysis/ implements the graph neural network (GNN) framework. For each sample of the MERFISH mouse cortex dataset, it builds a spatial k-nearest-neighbour cell graph (k = 20, Euclidean-distance edge weights). It then holds out one cell type at a time and trains a three-layer graph convolutional network (PyTorch Geometric) on one-hot cell-type features to predict which remaining cells sit next to the removed type. Evaluation is inductive, on held-out tissue sections, and performance is measured by ROC-AUC. Predictions are interpreted with Integrated Gradients (Captum) for node-level (cell-type) importance, tested against a permutation baseline with Mann–Whitney U tests and multiple-testing correction. GNNExplainer is used for edge-level (cell-type-pair) importance. (ii) spatial_regression/ contains Python and R notebooks that model spatially varying relationships in Xenium breast cancer data. They regress an EMT hallmark score on tumour-microenvironment and CNV-derived predictors, such as distances to neighbouring cell populations and principal components. The notebooks fit spatial error models (spreg), geographically weighted regression (mgwr) and multiscale GWR (GWmodel in R), with VIF/correlation filtering and variable-specific bandwidth selection. (iii) figure_plotting/ holds the notebook and conda environment that reproduce the paper’s GNN performance, node/edge importance and network figures from the saved outputs. Conda environment files ( base_env_gnn.yml , figures_paper_gnn.yml ) specify the dependencies. The other notebooks show analyses regarding the generalisability, contender frameworks, etc.

summary: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) can adapt O-RAN slice allocations to changing traffic and interference, but episode-average URLLC cost can hide failures during short traffic surges. We audit the maximum traffic-group mean cost; because the groups partition an episode, this worst-group constraint already implies the mean constraint. In a single-cell benchmark with burst traffic, selective jamming, impaired KPMs, and 105 discrete actions, 57 static actions satisfy the mean limit by point estimate but only 46 satisfy the worst-group limit on 100 fresh episodes; interval estimates classify 45 as supported, 10 as uncertain, and 50 as violating. The validation-selected mean-feasible action is worst-group uncertain on those traces. Across five seeds of PPO-Lagrangian, recurrent PPO-Lagrangian, and DQN, bootstrap intervals classify 13 of 15 final states as violating and two as uncertain; every recurrent final policy reduces to a constant catalogue action. A privileged oracle and a delayed-load heuristic, both a two-action rule tuned on validation episodes, safely recover about 4.2 return of adaptive headroom on training-matched and constant-jammer traces, which no evaluated learner or shield does. A calibrated risk ensemble has five supported evaluated runs on both scenarios, yet it loses return to the best safe static action and to the heuristic. Under an unseen sweep jammer, only 50% URLLC reservation remains supported. The resulting audit establishes traffic group, seed, checkpoint, and distribution shift as distinct dimensions of O-RAN DRL safety evaluation.

summary: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education requires sound instruments for identifying faculty development needs. This study reports the Portuguese adaptation and measurement-model evaluation of the Generative AI Competency Self-Efficacy Scale for Teachers and Researchers (GAICS-TR), a 35-item self-report instrument designed to assess academics’ perceived self-efficacy in relation to GenAI competencies. The scale comprises nine dimensions conceptually organised into four domains: Basic GenAI Understanding, Teaching with GenAI, Research with GenAI, and Professional Engagement with GenAI. The Portuguese version was developed through a pragmatic, team-based translation and adaptation procedure informed by established cross-cultural adaptation guidance. The procedure included translation of the items, review of their wording and contextual suitability, discussion of discrepancies, and consensus within the PRODIGIA research team. The items were administered on a five-point agreement scale to faculty and researchers from three partner universities, yielding 105 valid responses. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLSSEM) was used to assess indicator reliability, internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. The retained measurement model met the reported reliability and validity criteria, with the exception of the discriminant validity between GPD and GKG, which yielded a correlation of 0.923 (exceeding the standard 0.90 threshold). Item GPD2 was removed after presenting a loading of 0.482; after its removal, the professional-development dimension reached an Average Variance Extracted of 0.708 and a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.790. This item-level result should be interpreted cautiously because it may reflect wording, translation, or sample-specific effects. The adapted scale provides evidence for assessing self-reported GenAI competency self-efficacy in the participating institutions and for informing the diagnostic phase of PRODIGIA. Replication in larger, independent samples is needed.

This study reports the Portuguese adaptation and measurement-model evaluation of the Generative AI Competency Self-Efficacy Scale for Teachers and Researchers (GAICS-TR), a 35-item self-report instrument designed to assess academics’ perceived self-efficacy in relation to GenAI competencies. The scale comprises nine dimensions conceptually organised into four domains: Basic GenAI Understanding, Teaching with GenAI, Research with GenAI, and Professional Engagement with GenAI. The Portuguese version was developed through a pragmatic, team-based translation and adaptation procedure informed by established cross-cultural adaptation guidance. The procedure included translation of the items, review of their wording and contextual suitability, discussion of discrepancies, and consensus within the PRODIGIA research team. The items were administered on a five-point agreement scale to faculty and researchers from three partner universities, yielding 105 valid responses. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLSSEM) was used to assess indicator reliability, internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. The retained measurement model met the reported reliability and validity criteria, with the exception of the discriminant validity between GPD and GKG, which yielded a correlation of 0.923 (exceeding the standard 0.90 threshold). Item GPD2 was removed after presenting a loading of 0.482; after its removal, the professional-development dimension reached an Average Variance Extracted of 0.708 and a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.790. This item-level result should be interpreted cautiously because it may reflect wording, translation, or sample-specific effects. The adapted scale provides evidence for assessing self-reported GenAI competency self-efficacy in the participating institutions and for informing the diagnostic phase of PRODIGIA. Replication in larger, independent samples is needed.

summary: Version 1.8.1 carries the final revised manuscript (data and code availability, design history, and wording of the second wave) and adds means to the covariate summaries of the coverage audit. All other data are unchanged from version 1.8.0, and the measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. Version 1.8 accompanies the major revision of the manuscript. The results archive adds the dependency-graph coverage audit with its crawl, sample and eligibility records, the stratified sensitivity of the two waves, and the independent two-annotator validation of 400 items (packets, codebook, freeze records, the final annotators' pseudonymous answers, consensus and score). It also archives the cohort baselines, maintenance-scope entries and three table files that these analyses bind. The measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. The record contains two archives. pintrace-measurements-v1.tar.zst holds the per-repository measurement snapshots for 457 measured repositories and 301 matched control repositories, the archived upstream release evidence and the matched-control assignments. pintrace-results-v1.tar.zst holds the published result files, the formal-statistics outputs, the 150-item gold set, the research documentation, the manuscript PDF and LaTeX source, and the claim ledger that maps every rendered number to a result file and JSON pointer. Each archive includes a SHA-256 manifest and a README with extraction and reproduction instructions. The measurement files contain repository identifiers but no commit author names, commit messages, e-mail addresses or credentials. The code is at https://github.com/JunjieChen0/PinTrace under the MIT license. Replication data and results are released under CC BY 4.0. The study has no comparison group shielded from the incident, so the reported quantities describe timing, targets and persistence rather than an incident effect.
